The Judges (Inquiry) Bill, 2006
2. Thereafter, the Committee took up for discussions the Judges (Inquiry) Bill, 2006. Initiating
the discussion, the Chairman of the Committee observed that there was a doubt whether such a
Bill could be passed without a Constitutional amendment. Comparing the Judges (Inquiry) Bill, 2006
with the Judges (Inquiry) Act, 1968, he stated that the Parliament’s power to constitute an Inquiry
Committee was now proposed to be vested in the Judiciary, in the name of the National Judicial
Council, which amounted to usurping the existing powers of Parliament. V oicing his concern on
the issue, he observed, that in 1993 through a Judgment, the Judiciary took total authority onto
itself for taking its own decisions regarding appointments, which was not within the constitutional
parameters. He suggested for creating a body with representation from the Judiciary, Executive and
Bar, which could perform the work of a Screening Committee. This Committee could be named
as ‘‘Empowered Committee’’ and could be entrusted with the work of receiving petitions,
scrutinizing them to find out whether a prima-facie a case was made out against a Judge and
thereafter forward it to the National Judicial Council for inquiry. Thereafter, the Chairman raised
certain queries viz. (i) when a matter relating to a Judge of the Supreme Court is to be considered,
why should there be a representative of the High Courts; (ii) why couldn’t there be non-judicial
members such as the Vice-President of India, Speaker of Lok Sabha or any other authority in the
National Judicial Council?
3. Replying to the observations and queries of the Committee, the Secretary, Department of
Justice stated that there was in existence, a peer group oriented in-house mechanism, which was
being given statutory basis through the proposed Bill. He clarified that the issue of need for a
Constitutional Amendment was examined in depth by the Law Commission of India and that they
had come to a conclusion that the Constitution of the Proposed National Judicial Council, was not
an undesirable delegation of the authority of Parliament. Regarding the inclusion of non-judicial
members in the National Judicial Council, the Secretary stated that they have been guided by the
opinion of the Law Commission of India, which had concluded that a body of the nature of
National Judicial Council, the functions of which are confined to inquiry and investigation of
complaints against errant Judges, it should be with a Judicial body, comprising of Judicial people
alone. Regarding the need to enact a comprehensive legislation to go into the issues of
appointments, promotions and transfers, the representative of the Ministry stated that the present
Bill confined itself to the issue of inquiry and disciplinary action with a new feature of minor
measures, in addition to the removal process. He further stated that the Government had not gone
into the issues of appointments and transfers etc.
4. Thereafter, an Hon’ble Member of the Committee observed that since the issue involved
here was judicial accountability, the Committee was bound to look into the question of appointment
of Judges along with the questions of complaints or dealing with the complaints from people
against the Judges. The Member further observed that in 1993 through judicial interpretation of a
case, the Judiciary appropriated to itself the power to appoint, whereas in the world over, this

74
power has always been in the hands of the Executive. It was further observed that with the
provisions of this Bill, in addition to appointing themselves, the Judges would also be judging the
misbehaviour of their colleagues in the Judiciary, which would destroy the whole concept of
Judicial accountability. The member cautioned that if only the senior-most Judges were made the
Members of the National Judicial Council, they would be too occupied in dealing with the
complaints against their brother Judges and this could seriously interfere with their Judicial work
resulting in more pendency of cases and thus seriously hampering the dispensation of Justice.
5. Agreeing to the observation of the Member, another Hon'ble Member laid emphasis on
accountability and transparency. The Member wondered whether transparency could be maintained
in such an insulated Institution and more so when the provisions of the Right to Information Act
were not to apply to certain provisions of the Bill. Another Committee Member opined that the
Indian judicial system was a unique one which could not tolerate anybody interfering in the system.
Now, the National Judicial Council could not have non-judicial members. The Member further
observed that even the Chief Justice of India could not take any disciplinary action against a Judge
in spite of knowing that the Judge was involved in some corrupt practice. The only action
permitted under the Constitution being impeachment, there existed no supervisory control of the
Chief Justice of India over his subordinates.
6. Another Hon'ble Member, during the Committee’s deliberation on the Bill, raised the issue
of social justice in Judiciary. He opined that there was no proper representation of the SCs/STs/
Minorities/OBCs in the Judiciary. According to the Member this was the reason for lack of social
commitment on the part of the Judiciary. The Member suggested for the formation of a disciplinary
Committee consisting of Members from fields other than the Judiciary, as it was very unlikely that
a Judge would take action against a co-judge. The Member further opined that the Executive should
have a say in the appointment of Judges otherwise the Supreme Court Collegium will go on
recommending any name of their choice for appointment. Another Member of the Committee
favoured the idea of an ‘‘Empowered Committee’’ as the same, in his opinion, would save the
Judiciary from frivolous and vexatious complaints. The Member also opined that the Government,
which was a decision making body need not be bound by the opinion of the Law Commission.
Referring to the 1993 Judgement of the Supreme Court, the member observed that the Supreme
Court interpretated ‘‘Consultation’’ into ‘ ‘Command’’ which should to be corrected.
7. One Hon'ble Member disagreed with the idea of including all sections of the society in the
Council. The Member was also against allowing everybody to make a complaint against the judges
as this would undermine the independence of the Judiciary. The Member opined that there was an
urgent need for a comprehensive Bill dealing with all the aspects of Judiciary. Another Member
suggested that the Council for the appointment of Judges should be headed by the Vice-President
of India. Some Members of the Committee observed that there was inter-dependence in the
functioning of the three organs of the state, thus there was an urgent need, on the part of the
Judiciary, to commit itself to social equity. There was, however, general consensus among the
Committee Members that the Judiciary should be composed of men from different walks of life.
Therefore, the composition of the National Judicial Council should include people, other than
Judges.
8. Thereafter, the Chairman raised certain queries relating to the various provisions of the Bill
regarding (i) the consequences in case of difference of opinion among the members of the Council;
(ii) which Body to execute the order of the Council under Clause 20 of the Bill and (iii) the
consequences in case a Judge refused to obey the orders of the Council. The Committee desired
that the representative of the Department of Justice should clarify on these issues and also on the
issue of appointment, while dealing with the disciplinary aspect. The representative of the
Department of Justice assured the Committee that they would look into all the suggested aspects.

At the outset, the Chairman welcomed the Members and the representatives of the

2. Thereafter, the Committee took up the Clause-by-Clause consideration of the Judges
(Inquiry) Bill, 2006. On Clause 3 of the Bill, the Committee noted that the National Judicial Council,
though appointed by the President, totally excluded the presence of the Executive and the
Parliament. The Committee opined that this was a violation of the mandate given to the Parliament
under Article 124(4) of the Constitution of India. The Committee suggested inclusion of non-
Judicial Members in the Council to make it more broad based. The Committee further suggested
deletion of the words "to be nominated by Chief Justice of India" from sub Clauses (b) and
(c) of Clause 3(2) as it felt that by virtue of seniority, the Judges would automatically become the
Members of the Council. The Committee further suggested that the other members of the Council
should be appointed by the President and not by the Chief Justice of India. While deliberating upon
this particular Clause, the Committee suggested constitution of a separate Committee viz., the
‘‘Empowered Committee’’ as a screening body to initially screen the complaints both of the
individuals and the MPs.
3. Regarding Clauses 5 and 11 of the proposed Bill, the Committee observed that there was
no distinction in the procedures under the complaint procedure and the reference proceedure even
though the complaints were coming from two different sources viz. from individuals and 100/50
MPs Lok Sabha/Rajya Sabha. The Committee observed that the similarity of procedures could lead
to a situation where one individual would be at par with 100/50 MPs. The Committee opined that
the provisions of Clause 5 and 11 were delegating the powers of Parliament to the National Judicial
Council. The Committee took serious note of the fact that by virtue of the provisions of the
proposed Bill, there would be no distinction between an individual making a complaint under the
complaint procedure and 100/50MPs making complaints under reference procedure as per the
Constitutional provisions.
4. On Clause 8 of the Bill, the Committee noted that it sought to give a statutory basis to the
already existing in-House procedure which was being followed by the Judiciary since 1997,
whereby complaints against the Judges were decided by the Judges themselves. The Committee
further noted that this Clause was authorizing the proposed National Judicial Council to receive and
deal with the complaints. The Committee was in favour of setting up a Screening Committee to
initially scrutinize the complaints before they were referred to the National Judicial Council for
detailed investigation and inquiry.
5. Regarding Clause 9, the Committee observed that the provision was violative of the
principles of natural justice and the administrative law, which envisaged that the disciplinary
authority should not be the inquiry authority also. The Committee opined that investigation should
be done by some other independent, impartial authority.
6. On Clause 11 and 12 the Committee observed that since it had recommended the
Constitution of an ‘ ‘Empowered Committee’’ for initial screening and scrutiny of complaints under
both the complaint procedure and the reference procedure, hence both these Clauses should
accordingly be deleted. The Committee further observed that once the Empowered Committee was
brought into existence, the initial verification and screening of complaints could be done by it and
thereafter the work of investigation and inquiry could be carried out by the National Judicial
Council.
7. Regarding Clause 16, which stipulated appointment of an advocate by the Central
Government to conduct a case against a Judge, the Committee was in favour of including a
provision for legal aid to the Judge so that an equal opportunity of defending himself was accorded

80
to the judge. Clause 26 of the Bill also invited some discussion as it envisaged punishment for false
and vexatious complaints. The Committee felt that the provision was unnecessary and would deter
the people from making complaints. The Committee suggested inclusion of the words ‘‘after due
process of Inquiry’’ after the words ‘‘which is found by the Council’’ so as to provide a safeguard
to the Complainant.
8. Discussing Clause 30 of the Bill which provided for appeal against the order of removal
passed by the President or an order passed by the Council imposing minor measure, the Committee
observed that the Judges should not be treated as ordinary Government servants. The Committee
was of the categorical opinion that there should not be any appeal against the Presidential Order
of removal.
9. The Committee adopted the remaining Clauses without suggesting any changes therein as
they pertained to the procedural matters. As for the title of the Bill under Clause 1, the Committee
felt that if the title of the Bill was changed to ‘‘National Judicial Council Act’’ it would convey
the exact meaning of the proposed enactment. On the long title of the Bill, the Committee observed
that the inquiry against a Judge was by its very nature a sensitive matter, as being a matter against
the Constitutional Authority, therefore, the words ‘‘minor measures’’ should be substituted with the
words ‘‘appropriate measures’’.

13. ( 1) Where it is alleged that the Judge is unable to discharge
the duties of his office efficiently due to any physical or mental incapacity
and the allegation is denied, the Council may arrange for the medical
examination of the Judge by such Medical Board as may be appointed for
the purpose and the Judge shall submit himself to such medical examination
within the time specified in this behalf by the Council.
(2) The Medical Board shall undertake such medical examination
of the Judge as may be considered necessary and submit a report to the
Council stating therein whether the incapacity is such as to render the
Judge unfit to continue in office.
(3) If the Judge refuses to undergo medical examination
considered necessary by the Medical Board, it shall submit a report to the
Council stating therein the examination which the Judge has refused to
undergo, and the Council may, on receipt of such report, presume that the
Judge suffers ftom such physical or mental incapacity as is alleged.
(4) If the Judge agrees to undergo medical examination considered
necessary by the Medical Board, the said Board may permit him to
produce such other medical reports or opinions of experts as the Judge
deems it necessary to prove that he does not suffer from any physical or
mental incapacity, and thereafter the Medical Board shall submit a report
to the Council with its findings based upon the medical examination
conducted at the instance of the Board as well as the material produced
by the Judge as aforesaid.
(5) The Council may, after considering the written statement of
the Judge, the medical report submitted by the Medical Board and the

STATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS
A suitable legislative framework is the need of the hour for empowering a
judicial forum to deal with complaints against Judges of the Supreme Court and
High Courts. On the basis of the recommendations made in the 195th Report of
the Law Commission of India on the Judges (Inquiry) Bill, 2005, the Bill, namely
the Judges (Inquiry) Bill, 2006 has been prepared.
2. It may be recalled that the Judges (Inquiry) Act, 1968 was enacted with
a view to lay down a procedure for removal for proved misbehaviour or incapacity
of Judges of the High Courts and the Supreme Court by way of address of the
Houses of Parliament by the President. The Law Commission of India in its 195th
Report has examined the issue of judicial accountability in the light of the law laid
down by the Supreme Court in its various judgments, which relate to the
interpretation of articles 121, 124 and 217 of the Constitution.
3. The Bill, namely, the Judges (Inquiry) Bill, 2006 is based on the premise
that judicial independence is one of the basic fundamentals of the Constitution.
Judicial independence and judicial accountability are inseparable. Thus, there is an
urgent need of a legislation for establishing a National Judicial Council to look into
the allegations of misbehaviour or incapacity of a Judge of the Supreme Court or
of a High Court, as the case may be, and to regulate the procedure for such
investigation, inquiry and proof in a complaint procedure in addition to the earlier
‘‘reference procedure’’ as contained in the Judges (Inquiry) Act, 1968. In a
complaint procedure, a complaint can be made by any person to the Judicial
Council against Judges of the Supreme Court (except the Chief Justice of India),
Chief Justices and Judges of High Courts. The Judges (Inquiry) Bill, 2006, inter
alia, seeks to empower the National Judicial Council for imposing minor measures
also. The Bill also seeks to repeal the Judges (Inquiry) Act, 1968.
4. The Bill seeks to achieve the above objects.

NOTES ON CLAUSES
Clause 2 is the definition clause and it defines for the purposes of certainty
in the interpretation of the legislation ‘‘Code of Conduct’’ as the guidelines issued
by the Council under sub-section (1) of section 36, ‘‘complaint procedure’’ as a
procedure that is initiated by way of complaint; ‘‘incapacity’’ as ‘‘physical or
mental incapacity’’ that is likely to be of a permanent character; ‘‘inquiry’’ as
inquiry for proof of misbehavior or incapacity; ‘‘misbehavior’’ as wilful or persistent
conduct which brings dishonour or disrepute to the judiciary, or wilful or persistent
failure to perform the duties of a Judge or wilful abuse of judicial office, corruption,
lack of integrity, moral turpitude and includes violation of Code of Conduct; and
‘‘reference procedure’’ as procedure which is initiated by way of a motion for
removal which is referred by the Speaker or the Chairman under sub-section (2)
of section 11.
Clause 3 provides for establishment of National Judicial Council consisting
of (a) the Chief Justice of India – Chairperson; (b) two senior-most Judges of the
Supreme Court to be nominated by the Chief Justice of India – Members; and
(c) two Chief Justices of the High Courts to be nominated by the Chief Justice of
India – Members.
Clause 4 provides for composition of the Council to change in certain
circumstances when the allegations are against the Chief Justice of India, he shall
not take part in the proceedings of the Council. Where allegations are against the
member of the Council or they recuse themselves. The President in the case of the
Chief Justice of India and the Chief Justice of India in case of Members shall
nominate another member for the purpose of investigation and inquiry.
Clause 5 provides for functions of the Council to investigate and inquire
into the allegation of misbehaviour or incapacity against the Judge of the Supreme
Court or Judge of a High Court.
Clause 6 provides for the Council to conduct the investigation and inquiry
into any act or conduct of any person other than a Judge in so far as the Council
considers it necessary.
Clause 7 provides for appointment of officers and employees of the Council
for the purposes of discharge of its functions and to fix their terms and conditions
of service. It also provides for the utilisation of the services of any officer or
employee of the Government or any other agency.
Clause 8 provides the procedure for making a complaint involving allegations
of misbehaviour or incapacity in respect of a Judge. It also provides for the
particulars to be given in such complaint.
Clause 9 provides the procedure for verification and preliminary investigation
of the complaints. It also provides for the dismissal of frivolous and vexatious
complaints.

FINANCIAL MEMORANDUM
Clause 3 of the Bill provides for establishment of National Judicial Council
comprising of Chief Justice of India as the Chairperson and Judges of the Supreme
Court and the Chief Justices of High Courts as members.
Clause 7 of the Bill provides for appointment of a Secretary and such other
officers and employees as the President may determine from time to time in
consultation with the Council.
Clause 16 of the Bill empowers the Central Government if requested by the
Council to appoint an advocate to conduct the case against the Judge.
At this stage, it is not possible to give an estimate of expenditure involved
(recurring and non-recurring). However, the expenditure would be met from the

MEMORANDUM REGARDING DELEGATED LEGISLATION
Clause 37(4) empowers the Joint Committee of both the Houses of Parliament
to frame rules for providing the form in which a complaint under sub-section (1)
of section 8 may be made.
Clause 22 provides for the manner of presentation of address to the

administrative details and it is not practicable to provide for them in the Bill itself.

in Section 9 also.
(v) The proposed legislation
do not empower the
Council to take any action
pending conclusion of the
inquiry.

131
ANNEXURE-C
SUMMARY OF VIEWS RECEIVED FROM
V ARIOUS HIGH COURTS
1. Calcutta The proposed Bill aims at destructing the basic features of the
Constitution of India and deprives the citizens of this country of
their legal remedy through an independent Judicial System.
2. Himachal Pradesh The provisions of the Bill hit upon the basic structure of the
Constitution and have the potential of impinging upon as well as
eroding the independence of Judiciary. If put to practice and
implementation, these provisions would shake the people’s
confidence and faith in judicial system which ultimately can
prejudice the democratic judicial system.
3. Orissa No objection to the provisions made in the Bill. However, it is
suggested that section 26 of the Bill may be suitably amended to
make the penal provision more rigorous and complaint may be
defined in the Bill.
4. Andhra Pradesh Keeping in view the nature of the proposed enactment, it is not
proper for the High Court to express any view.
5. Sikkim The proposed Bill, if enacted, will ruin the independence of the
Judiciary and once the provisions are put into effect, the Judiciary
of India, as known hereunto will cease to exist. The Bill should be
scrapped in toto.
6. Jharkhand The proposed legislation shall cause harm and lower down the
dignity and majesty of the Judiciary having an adverse effect on the
independence of higher judiciary.
The ultimate object can be achieved by the “in house peer review”
which can be further tonned up and made more effective.
There is no regulatory check for receiving the complaint. Any
person can lodge a complaint in writing with simple verification.
Further, any complaint from any other source can be entertained.
This situation may cause immense injury and damage to the prestige
and dignity of the person (Section 8).
The nature of verification of preliminary investigation has not been
properly classified (Section 9).
The number of members has been arbitrarily fixed, [Section 11
(a & b)].
There is no provision for appointing an advocate in defence (Section
16).
131

132
In case of any proved charges, the only measure should be, as
provided under clause (iv) of Section 20 as for any proved
allegation continuation of such person is not desirable in such a high
office.
Provisions in clause (d) Section 23 would amount a multiple
punishment. Further punishment would offend Articles 14 & 21 of
the Constitution.
Keeping the identity confidential from one against whom the
complaint is made would amount to denial of opportunity of
effective defence and will be violative of the principles of natural
justice.
The provisions of the Act should not be made applicable to those,
who were appointed when there was no such legislation.
7. Allahabad The proposed Judges (Inquiry) Bill, 2006 is in utter disregard to the
basic structure of the Constitution and would erode the
independence of the Judiciary. It will only harm the judicial system
and is bound to shake people’s confidence and faith ruining our
democracy. Thus, it should be denounced strongly.
The Judges (Inquiry) Bill, 2006 contains various provisions, which
are contrary to the law laid down by the Apex Court in different
cases.
The Constitution of India, Article 124 provides for establishments
and constitution of the Supreme Court. Article 217 provides for
appointment and conditions of the office of a Judge of the High
Court. Article 124(4) provides that a Judge of the Supreme Court
shall not be removed from the office except by an order of the
President passed after an address by each House of Parliament
supported by a majority of the total membership of that House and
by a majority of not less than two third of the members of the
House present and voting has been presented to the President in the
same session for such removal on the ground of proved
misbehaviour of incapacity. Article 124( 5) provides that Parliament
may by law regulate the procedure for the presentation of an
address and for the investigation and proof of the misbehaviour or
incapacity of a Judge under clause (4). According to Article 217(1)
proviso (b) a Judge of a High Court may be removed from the
office by the President in the manner provided in clause (4) of
Article 124. The Office of the judge of the Supreme Court or the
High Court is a constitutional office. The tenure of the office of a
Judge is secured under the Constitutional office. The tenure of the
office of a judge is secured under the Constitution with object and
purpose to maintain independence of  judiciary.
The Apex Court in (1995)6 S.C.C. 765; Union of India and others
vs. Pratibha Bonnerjes and another, held that a Judge of  the
Higher Judiciary occupies a unique position under the Constitution.
He would not be able to discharge his duties without fear or favour

133
unless he is totally independent of the Executive, which he would
not be if he is regarded as a government servant.
The independence of Judiciary is the essence and basic structure of
the Constitution. It is well settled by a series of  Constitutional Bench
judgments of this Court that judicial independence is a basic
structure of the Constitution which could not be tinkered with
by Parliament even in exercise of its amending power under
Article 368.
The Parliament in exercise of its power under Article 124(5) of the
Constitution of India has enacted the Judges (Inquiry) Act, 1968
which contains the provisions regulating the procedure for
presentation of an address and for the investigation and proof of
the misbehaviour or incapacity of a Judge. The Judges (Inquiry)
Bill, 2006 shows the noticeable departure from the earlier 1968 Act
and contains various clauses, which erode the independence of
Judiciary.
The Judges (Inquiry) Bill, 2006 contains various clauses, which fall
beyond the legislative power given to Parliament under Article
225(5) of the Constitution. There are various clauses in the Judges
(Inquiry) Bill, 2006, which will erode the independence of Judiciary
and make the Judges of the High Courts and the Supreme Court
subservient to another body and they will function under constant
fear of investigation and inquiry on any complaint made by anyone
with varied reasons.
In the constitution of the Council as contemplated under Clause 3(2)
of the Bill the Chief Justice of the concerned High Court is not
made a member. In case of investigation of misbehaviour or
incapacity of a Judge of the High Court, the Chief Justice of that
High Court has to be necessarily included as a member of the
Committee.
Clause 4(3) of Chapter-II refers to about the allegations made in a
complaint by any person against a Judge of the Supreme Court or
the High Court. The complaint by any person against a Judge of the
Supreme Court or the High Court is not envisaged in the
Constitution and permitting such complaint shall be against the
constitutional scheme.
Chapter-III, while providing a procedure of complaint by any person
against misbehaviour or incapacity in respect of a Judge to the
Council is contrary to the constitutional provisions and the scheme.
The Constitution does not contemplate the complaint of any kind
against a Judge. The procedure for investigation and proof of
misbehaviour or incapacity of a Judge follows only when motion is
brought in each House of Parliament alleging any such misbehaviour
or incapacity.
The Procedure for permitting complaints against a Judge will be
prejudicial to fearless functioning of judges of the Higher Judiciary.

134
There will be a spate of complaints by litigants and lawyers of the
loosing party against the Judges. Our judicial system provides for
correction of the judgment by review, appeal and other mechanism.
The complaint procedure as envisaged in the Judges (Inquiry)
Bill, 2006 will expose every Judge to false and baseless complaints.
Considerable time of the Judges shall be taken in giving their
comments to such complaints which are likely to be filed looking to
the nature of the job which is being performed by the Judges. The
Judge shall always be under constant fear for being subjected to a
complaint whenever he decides a case.
A Constitution Bench of the Apex Court while interpreting Article
124(4) and 124(5) of the Constitution held that there cannot be any
machinery to enquire into the integrity of its Judges except the
constitutional machinery for removal of a Judge. The Bill permitting
complaint by any person against a Judge and investigation and proof
of such complaint by the National Judicial Council is against the
constitutional scheme and the law declared by the Apex Court.
Again, the Apex Court in C. Ravichandran Iyer vs. Justice A.M.
Bhattacharjee and others, reiterated that founding fathers of the
Constitution advisedly adopted a cumbersome process of
impeachment as a mode to remove a Judge. The Constitution does
not permit any action by any agency other than initiation of action
under Article 124(4) of the Constitution by the Parliament.
The Apex Court itself has laid down that the Chief Justice of a high
Court has ample power to deal with any Judge who misconduct
himself. Self regulation by Judiciary is the method which has been
emphasized by the Apex Court. The in-house remedy for restoring
the confidence of the people against errant behaviour or misconduct
by any Judge has functioned quite effectively.
The Chief Justice of India being head of the Judicial fraternity does
not lack means and power to discipline the Judges. The gap
between proved misbehaviour and bad behaviour inconsistent with
high office can only be disciplined by self regulation through an in-
house procedure as laid down by the Apex Court in C. Ravichandran
Iyer’s cases.
The provisions of the Bill in Chapter II providing for entertaining
private complaints and investigation of such complaints and action
thereof by the Council is contrary to the constitutional scheme,
independence of Judiciary and the law of land as laid down by the
Apex Court. Thus, the provisions of Clauses 8, 9, 10 and 11 of
Chapter-III, which permit entertainment of individual complaint by
any person and proceedings thereupon is completely against the
constitutional scheme and hampers fearless discharge of function by
a Judge.
The investigation regarding incapacity (physical or mental) can be
presented only in accordance with the procedure prescribed in the
constitution, i.e., only after a motion is admitted in Parliament.

135
Clause 13 is also not in accord with the constitutional scheme and
shall lead to undue interference in functioning of a judge.
Clause 20 of the Judges (Inquiry) Bill, 2006 gives power to the
Council to impose minor punishment (measures) on a Judge when
the Council is of the opinion that the charges do not warrant
removal. In the Constitution there is no concept of awarding any
minor punishment on a such high constitutional office. The
Constitution of India does not contemplate the office of a Judge of
the High Court or Supreme Court as a service nor the Constitution
of India empowers the Parliament to lay down a service condition
of the Judges of the High court or Supreme Court. The National
Judicial Council is proposed to substitute the Committee of three
Judges provided in the Judges (Inquiry) Act, 1968. The Committee
is set up only for purposes of investigation and proof of
misbehaviour or incapacity of a Judge as provided under Article
124(5).
The concept of awarding minor measures violates the constitutional
scheme and is contrary to the concept of independence of Judiciary.
The constitutional protection to Judges is not for their personal
benefit but to protect the Judiciary and its independence, which is
in larger public interest.
The Constitution itself with regard to other constitutional office
provides the concept of suspension. It is deliberately not provided
with regard to office of the Judges of the High Courts and the
Supreme Court.
Clause 18 provides that even the identity of the complainant shall be
kept confidential from the Judge against whom complaint is made
out. This provision is wholly arbitrary and against the constitutional
scheme. Firstly no individual can be permitted to file a complaint
against a judge and secondly keeping the identity of the complainant
confidential from the Judge concerned will be against the principles
of natural justice.
Clause 29 of the Judges (Inquiry) Bill, 2006 empowers the Council
during the pendency of the investigation or impeachment, stoppage
of assigned judicial work to the Judge concerned. While interpreting
the constitutional provisions of Articles 124(4) and 124(5) the
submission that the Judge can be restrained from performing his
judicial functions during pendency of the impeachment proceedings
was specifically rejected by the Constitution Bench of the Apex
Court. In sub-Committee on Judicial Accountability case, it was held
that when the power of stopping the Judge from functioning cannot
be exercised during pendency of the impeachment proceedings in
the Parliament, the Council cannot stop assignment of judicial work
during investigation on a private complaint.
Clause 37 empowers the joint Committee of both houses of
Parliament to make rules to carry out the purpose of the Act. Clause
37(4) indicates the matters on which the Committee can frame

136
rules, which include manner of transmission of motion, manner of
presentation of an address to the President and the other matters.
Article 124(5) mandates that it is the Parliament which may regulate
the proceeding for presentation of an address and allegation of proof
of misbehaviour. It is only the Parliament which by law regulate the
procedure for presentation of an address and for the investigation.
The said power to make law cannot be delegated or assigned to any
other body including the Committee.
V arious provision of the Judges (Inquiry) Bill, 2006 are against the
basic feature of the Constitution. The independence of Judiciary
being one of the accepted basic feature the provisions of the Judges
(Inquiry) Bill, 2006, if enacted into an Act, shall erode the basic
feature of the Constitution.
The in-house procedure in the Judiciary itself is sufficient protection
for minor abrasion and any misconduct. Rules of every High Court
authorize the Chief Justice to allocate work to other Judges. The
power of allocation of work to Chief Justice contains enough power
to control the Judges’ functioning and discharge of their duties.
7. Punjab and Haryana The proposed Judges (Inquiry) Bill, 2006 not only lack constitutional
back-up, but it also is a devise to nail the independence of the
judiciary. Clause (5) of Article 124 of the Constitution permits
Parliament to enact law to regulate the procedure for the
investigation and proof of the misbehaviour or incapacity of a Judge
under Clause (4) thereof. Thus, the law to be enacted in exercise
of powers under Article 124(5) of the Constitution is to regulate the
procedure as to how an inquiry into the alleged misbehaviour or
incapacity of a Judge, on the basis of which Parliament can
recommend his removal from the Office under Article 124( 4), is to
be conducted. Clause (5) of Article 124 does not permit the
Parliament to introduce an Authority to determine misbehaviour or
incapacity of a Judge other than what the Constitution has provided
under Clause (4) of Article 124.
The proposed Bill has introduced an authority alien to our
constitutional scheme and proposes to create an authority not
envisaged by the Constitution under Clause (4) of Article 124. The
provision, asking a Judge to seek voluntary retirement or withdrawal
of judicial work is virtual removal from the office for all intents and
purposes and, thus, lacks constitutional sanctions.
No law can be enacted which may attempt to erode the
independence of the Judiciary. The residual law making power is not
available with Parliament especially when for issues like salary,
privileges, allowances and determination of age etc., it has been
expressly authorized to enact law under Articles 124, 125, 217 &
218 of the Constitution of India.
The power and strength of the Judiciary lies in public faith, enjoined
upon by it. It will not be possible for a Judges to work fairly and
fearlessly during the rest of his service tenure once he is issued

137
“warnings” or his judicial work is withdrawn albeit for a small
length of period. The censure or public admonition will take away
the moral authority with a judge to hold the Office.
Under the Constitutional scheme, the Judges of the High Courts are
not administratively subordinate to the Supreme court. Both the
institutions are independent of each other and exercise their judicial
powers within the well defined parameters. The Supreme Court
enjoys appellate judicial powers. The proposed Bill, on the contrary,
be-littles the position of High Court Judges and makes them
subordinate and amenable to the administrative control of the Judges
of the Supreme Court.
8. Madhya Pradesh The Bill makes serious and decisive inroads into constitutional
freedom conferred on the judges by permitting all and sundry to file
a complaint and by conferring power on the council to suo motu
take cognizance of any act which they feel needs to be corrected.
The Bill is against the basic structure of the Constitution which
envisages that the High Court and the Supreme Court Judges shall
have absolute freedom and independence in the performance of their
duties and that the High Court Judges are not subordinate to the
Supreme Court Judges and that they shall not be treated as common
government servants.
The complaint proceedure contained in Chapter III  and provision
for imposition of measures in Section 20 (1) (b) will seriously
affect the independence of the judiciary and will be inconsistent
with clause (4) and (5) of Article 124 and Article 218 of the
Constitution.
The in-house procedure developed by the Supreme Court is enough
to tackle aberrations not meriting impeachment in the conduct of
judges.
The Bill is contrary to specific provisions of the Constitution which
provides for appointment of a Judge and his removal from office
by the President by a specific procedure in the House. The
Constitution has specifically omitted to prescribe any procedure
for taking any disciplinary action by imposing lesser punishments.
From the scheme of the Constitution and various judgments of the
Supreme Court, it is clear that Judges are not subordinate to the
Chief Justice, the Parliament or to any Authority. The Bill seeks to
introduce a disciplinary authority/body to sit over the Judges and to
take disciplinary action against them.
The Bill is a deliberate measure to subvert the judicial independence
and individual independence of the judges as it seeks to create an
extra-constitutional body like the council with full power to control
and regulate the functioning and conduct of the judges.
The very concept of the Bill is misconceived as it seeks to vest the
supreme authority in the Chief Justice of India as if it is the
appointing, disciplinary authority of all the Judges in the country.

138
9. Chhattisgarh The full co urt unanimously resolved to oppose the Bill.
10. Gujarat The provisions of the Bill would erode the independence of the
judiciary, result in interference in the independent functioning of the
Courts and would also come in the way of the Judges of the
Supreme Court and of the High Courts in the performance of their
duties without fear or favour, affection or ill-will. Everyday, Judges
decide cases in which one of the parties is a loser. Our judicial
system provides for correction of the judgment by appeal, review
and other mechanisms, but the procedure as envisaged in
Chapter III of the Judges (Inquiry) Bill, 2006 will expose every
Judge to false and baseless complaints. Considerable time of the
Judges will be consumed in giving their comments to such
complaints which are likely to be filed looking to the nature of the
duties being performed by the Judges. Judges shall always be in
constant fear of being subjected to complaints whenever they decide
cases.
The Apex Court has held in Sub-Committee on Judicial
Accountability Vs. Union of India & Ors., (1991) 4 SCC 699 that
there cannot be any machinery to inquire into the integrity of a
Judge of the Higher Judiciary except the constitutional machinery
for removal of Judge.
The Constitution permits removal of a Judge only when the motion
is carried with requisite majority of both the Houses of Parliament
recommending to the President for removal of the Judge. In other
words, the Constitution does not permit any action by any agency
other than the initiation of an action under Article 124(4) or Article
217(1)(b) read with Article 124(4), as the case may be.
The Apex Court has laid down that the Chief Justice of the High
Court has ample power to deal with any Judge for any misconduct
or deviant behaviour not warranting impeachment. The
Constitutional scheme does not concede any such power to any
other authority.
While there are express provisions in the Constitution empowering
the Parliament/President to lay down the conditions of service of
holders of other constitutional offices, there is a marked and
deliberate absence of any such provisions with regard to laying
down conditions of service of Judges of the High Courts and the
Supreme Court except for the limited purpose of salaries and
allowances and rights in respect of leave of absence and pensions
as laid down in Article 125 and 221 and for the purpose of
regulating the procedure for impeachment under Article 124( 4) and
(5). It is, therefore, abundantly clear that Constitution never
contemplated the parliament to make law for imposing any minor
measure on the Judges of the Supreme Court or the High Courts.

INTRODUCTION
I, the Chairman of the Committee on Personnel, Public Grievances, Law and Justice, having
been authorised by the Committee to submit this Report on its behalf, do hereby present its Twenty
Second Report on the Gram Nyayalayas Bill, 2007. The Bill seeks to establish Gram Nyayalayas
for the purpose of providing access to justice, both civil and criminal, to the citizens at the grass-
roots level and to ensure that opportunities for securing justice are not denied to any citizen by
reason of social, economic or other disabilities.
2. In pursuance of the rules relating to the Department Related Parliamentary Standing
Committee, the Hon’ble Chairman, Rajya Sabha referred
♣  the Bill, as introduced in the Rajya Sabha
on the 15th May, 2007 and pending therein, to this Committee on the 17th May, 2007 for
examination and report.
3. Keeping in view the importance of the Bill, the Committee decided to issue a press
communique to solicit views/suggestions from desirous individuals/organisations on the provisions
of the Bill. Accordingly, a press communique was issued in response to which memoranda
containing suggestions were received by the Committee.
4. The Committee heard the oral evidence of the Secretary, Legislative Department, Ministry
of Law and Justice in its meetings held on 7th and 14th June, 2007.
5. While considering the Bill, the Committee took note of the following documents/information
placed before it: —
(i) Background note on the Bill;
(ii) The comments of the Legislative Department on the views/suggestions contained in the
memoranda received from various organisations/institutions/individuals/experts on the
provisions of the Bill;
(iii) Suggestions given by some State Governments with whom the Committee held
discussions on the Bill; and
(iv) Suggestions of the Secretary, Ministry of Panchayati Raj.
6. The Committee held clause-by-clause consideration of the Bill on the 16th August, 2007.
7. The Committee adopted the Report in its meeting held on the 29th August, 2007.
8. For the facility of reference and convenience, the observations and recommendations of the
Committee have been printed in bold letters in the body of the Report.

1
REPORT
The Gram Nyayalayas Bill, 2007 (Annexure-A) seeks to establish Gram Nyayalayas for the
purpose of providing access to justice, both civil and criminal, to the citizens at the grass-roots
level and to ensure that opportunities for securing justice are not denied to any citizen by reason
of social, economic or other disabilities and for matters connected therewith or incidental thereto.
2. The Gram Nyayalayas Bill, 2007 was introduced* in the Rajya Sabha on 15th May, 2007.
It was referred
♣ by the Chairman, Rajya Sabha to the Department Related Parliamentary Standing
Committee on Personnel, Public Grievances, Law and Justice on 17th May, 2007 for examination
and report.
3. The background note, furnished by the Ministry of Law and Justice, on the Bill, stated as
follows:
“Article 39 A of the Constitution of India directs the State to secure that the operation of
the legal system promotes justice, on a basis of equal opportunity, and shall, in particular,
provide free legal aid, by suitable legislation or schemes or in any other way, to ensure that
opportunities for securing justice are not denied to any citizen by reason of economic or
other disabilities. The Government has taken various measures to strengthen judicial system,
inter alia, by simplifying the procedural laws; incorporating various alternative dispute
resolution mechanisms such as arbitration, conciliation and mediation, conducting of Lok
Adalats, etc. The Law Commission of India in its 114th Report on Gram Nyayalayas
suggested establishment of Gram Nyayalayas so that speedy, inexpensive and substantial
justice could be provided to the common man. The Gram Nyayalayas Bill, 2007 is broadly
based on the recommendations of the Law Commission. The Gram Nyayalayas Bill, 2007
after its enactment as an Act of Parliament would ensure justice to the poor at their
doorstep. Setting up of Gram Nyayalayas with mobility in the rural areas would bring to
the people of rural areas speedy, affordable and substantial justice.”
4. The Committee decided to invite views/suggestions from desirous individuals/organisations
on the Bill. It, accordingly, authorised the Secretariat to issue a press release inviting views/
suggestions. In response to the press release published in major English and Hindi dailies and
vernacular newspapers all over India on 3rd June, 2007, a number of representations/memoranda
were received.
4.1 The Committee forwarded the memoranda so received from the individuals and
organisations to the Ministry of Law and Justice (Legislative Department) for their comments
thereon. The comments of the Ministry were received on 14th August, 2007(Annexure-B).
4.2 The major points raised in the memoranda are summarized as follows:
(i) Clause 3(1) of the Bill envisages Gram Nyayalayas at intermediate level. This might
reduce accessibility to justice through these Nyayalayas as the litigant would have to
travel from the village to the block at the expense of time and money.
(ii) R eservation should be made mandatory. The benefit of reservation may be extended to
Backward Class of citizens also.

(iii) If the Magistrate transfers the case to his own court as per Clause 25 at the last stage,
the trial will get delayed resulting in pendency of cases.
(iv) Since lawyers are not barred, the same procedures will creep in as in the case of
formal judicial set up.
(v) One of the conciliators provided in Clause 30(3) should be a woman.
(vi) Clause 32 would bring in th e same rigidity and procedural aspects which exist in the
formal judicial set up.
(vii) Practical difficulties as to availability of legally qualified persons, their dependability as
to being stationed in a rural location, the heavy burden to be borne by the exchequer
will be faced. Expenditure will have to be incurred to hold mobile courts and court
proceedings in villages and for providing accommodation to Nyayadhikaris and other
staff.
(viii) Gram Nyayadhikari may be treated a part of the cadre of State Subordinate Judicial
Service and it may be the first point of entry in that service. This would ensure their
career progression and would attract good talent.
(ix) Provision should be made insisting that there should be at least one sitting of Gram
Nyayadhikari at each headquarters of Gram Nyayalayas every month.
(x) The recruitment of Nyayadhikaris of Gram Nyayalaya may be made through Union
Public Service Commission. After recruitment, the qualified candidate may be provided
extensive training at the National Judicial Academy at Bhopal.
(xi) Instead of setting up Gram Nyayalayas at the intermediate panchayat level, the need of
the hour is to strengthen the existing system of subordinate judiciary, which forms the
major chunk of our judicial system, by creating additional courts at the
District/Tehsil/Taluka level depending upon the extent of pendency of cases to ensure
that the litigants get quick justice at reasonable cost. This can be done over a period
of, say, five years. Simultaneously, the High Courts need to effectively review and
monitor the progress of disposal of cases by subordinate judiciary on regular basis.
This will entail much less expenditure on the creation of additional infrastructure at the
District/Tehsil/Taluka level than on the creation of Gram Nyayalayas. In addition, the
strength of Judges in the High Courts and the Supreme Court must also be increased
to ensure that the disposal of cases gets speeded up to a reasonable extent. Also, we
must lay much greater emphasis on the creation of alternative redressal mechanism.
(xii) In addition to the provision for appeal included in the Bill, a provision for revision may
also be included. It may be noted that inspite of the fact that there is no provision
of appeal from the Senior Civil Judge or Additional/Assistant Sessions Judge, High
Court may exercise its jurisdiction under Articles 226 and 227 of the Constitution.
4.3 The highlights of the response of the Legislative Department on the comments/suggestions
contained in the memoranda are as under:
(i) Nyaya Panchayats established by various State Governments under the provisions of
respective State Panchayati Raj legislations are already functioning. The concept of
establishment of Gram Nyayalayas are different from Nyaya Panchayats.
(ii) Gram Nyayalayas, like other subordinate judiciary, will be under direct control of the
respective High Courts.

3
(iii) The approach through this legislation is that simple and non-complicated disputes
which could be resolved in a short time will be entrusted to the Gram Nyayalayas.
Endeavour is made to make the Gram Nyayalayas to be effective forum for resolution
of disputes emanating from rural areas and to deal with such disputes, the Gram
Nyayalayas will follow the summary procedure as laid down under the procedural
codes.
(iv) Establishing Gram Nyayalayas at every Gram Panchayat level would involve a huge
expenditure, which is very difficult for the Central Government as well as the State
Government to meet. To manage the Gram Nyayalayas financially, it was felt not
feasible to consider establishing Gram Nyayalayas at every Gram Panchayat level but
only at intermediate Panchayat level. However, anticipating such difficulties, the
concept of mobile Courts has been incorporated in clause 11 of the Bill.
(v) Wide publicity about the objects and scope of the Gram Nyayalayas Bill, 2007 has
already been given. The same course would be adopted by the Central Government/
State Government after its enactment.
5. The Committee heard the views of the State Governments of Uttarakhand, Madhya Pradesh,

Maharashtra and NCT of Delhi responded and the gist of their views are as follows:—
I. Gujarat
(i) Taking into consideration the provisions of the said Bill, it appears that the State

there are 225 Talukas in the State. Accordingly, 225 Nyayadhikaris will be required to
be appointed and if the strength of each of these courts is temporarily placed as 21,
then in all, 4725 new posts will be required to be created and in view of the provisions

inter alia provides that the Nyayadhikari will be required to hold mobile courts and
conduct proceedings in villages. To ensure this, the Nyayadhikaris will have to be
provided with mobile vans, drivers etc. Further, the State Government will have to
see that the Nyayadhikaris and other staff are provided with accommodation and as
such, the State Government will have to undertake the construction of Government
quarters for them. Other infrastructure facilities will also be required to be provided
to the said Gram Nyayalaya. The State Government is therefore, of the view that
for providing such infrastructure facilities, a huge amount running into crores of
rupees which may exceed Rs. 300 crores will have to be spent by the State
Government. The State Government is of the view that it would a huge burden on the
State Exchequer.
(ii) They have submitted that they are enforcing the scheme of evening Courts, the system
of Alternative Dispute Resolution and the concept of Lok Adalats. It has also been
submitted that a scheme called “Tirth Gram Yojna” has been implemented for rural
Gujarat to encourage communal harmony and brotherhood at village level. As regards
the financial burden on the State exchequer, it has been stated that there is a foreseen
additional financial burden which is amounting to approximately Rs. 300 crores and
that at present, budgetary provisions for the Legal Department is Rs. 257 crores.

II. Uttarakhand
(i) There are 95 Panchayats of medium-level in the State. Therefore, 25 Gram Nyayalayas

Rs. 1 crore is likely to be spent for the construction of one building for Gram
Nyayalaya and a residential house for Nyayadhikari. A recurring expenditure of about
Rs. 10 lacs per annum would be incurred on one Gram Nyayalaya. Government of
India have already provided recurring and non-recurring amount for Fast Track

(ii) As there are less number of criminal and civil disputes in the villages of Uttarakhand,

(iii) The system of mobile courts seems suitable for the geographical conditions of

(iv) This should also be provided in the proposed Bill as to how Gram-Nyayalayas will

(v) It has been provided in the proposed Bill that advocates can appear in Gram

(vi) In order to attract talented persons to the post of Nyayadhikari, it is necessary that

(i) In this context, it is submitted that in the National Capital Territory of Delhi, the
