numbers of complaints regarding faulty rolls, missing names etc. In such cases, a person
having a bonafide “Voter Identity Card” should have legal rights to vote. (Para 5.10)
Action Taken Reply
1.1 The Election Commission has set an initial time frame of 31.08.08 to complete the exercise
of photorolls. Some States/Union territories however, due to prevailing ground situation may need
more time. The Commission is closely monitoring the exercise. Due to prevailing circumstances,
PER is not being taken up in Assam, Jammu and Kashmir and Nagaland for the present.
1.2 According to the extant provisions of law (sub-section (1) of section 62 of the RP
Act, 1951), only those who are enrolled as an elector in the electoral roll of a constituency can
exercise their vote. Therefore, to be registered as a voter in electoral roll is the first and foremost
requirement for exercising the right to vote. EPIC are issued for the purpose of verification /
identification of the bonafide of that registered voter. Electors Photo Identity Card, once issued is
a valid identity for the purpose of exercising ones franchise irrespective of whether a person has
moved from place where EPIC was originally issued provided the person is registered as a voter
at that point of time in that place. On the date of poll, a person is allowed to vote in a particular
polling station of a constituency if his/her name is in the Electoral Roll and his/her identity is
established through a bonafide document (EPIC). For polling purposes, the basic document used
would be the Electoral Roll and EPIC is only an instrument of identification to ensure that the
person appearing in a polling station to vote is same what he claims to be. Every person who is,
for the time being entered in the electoral roll of any constituency shall be entitled to vote in that
constituency. Therefore, if the “V oter Identity Card” holder is enrolled in the electoral roll in force,
only then he can exercise his vote, otherwise not.
Committee’s further observation
1.3 The Committee’ s concern was that a registered voter having the valid voter identity card
should not be denied of his right to vote. It is the responsibility of the State to remove the
inaccuracy in the electoral rolls and that can be done by taking extra measures/precautions ensuring
16

17
that photo electoral rolls are free of errors. The Committee is keen to know what extra measures
have been taken to remove the errors and what has been its outcome.
Recommendation/observation
2. The Committee, while appreciating the efforts taken by the Commission in
computerization of the data for electoral rolls of the entire country, desires that feedback
reports on its use by the State CEOs may be procured and the level of satisfaction of the
working of the software communicated to the Committee. (Para 5.11)
Action Taken Reply
2.1 The Election Commission had not prescribed any common software for maintenance of
Electoral Roll in the country but had only prescribed the underlying data structure and the
processes. Each State has computerised the Electoral Rolls in accordance with the basic parameter
and structure laid down by the Commission.
Committee’s further observation
2.2 The Committee is not satisfied with the reply as the Committee was not apprised of the
feedback received from the State CEOs. The Committee desires to know the efforts made to get
that feedback and what action was taken by the EC. Whether at any time evaluation was made
to ensure the efficacy of the system. The Committee may be given the details.
Recommendation/observation
POST OFFICES FOR VERIFICA TION/REVISION OF ELECT ORAL ROLLS
3. The Committee is perturbed to know that the Election Commission has replied that
the Commission does not see the necessity of another office for electoral roll revision at
district level. The reason to stress for opening an office of Election Commission at district
level is for better monitoring and working as a facilitation center to the less educated
people living in rural areas/villages, for them registering their names means loosing one
day wages/earning. Every year there has been numerous complaints like missing names,
wrong entries, different photographs which speak a lot about the working of ERO/BDO. The
Committee feels that there is a need for it and to begin with the Election Commission
should at least on trial basis start establishing its offices for the purpose at the district
levels and district level officer would be made accountable for revision of the rolls. The
Committee further recommends that the Commission should set some target for the
purpose of revision of the electoral rolls. (Para 5.14)
Action Taken Reply
3.1 Revision of Rolls is done through a large number of EROs who are the statutory authorities
to prepare rolls. The manpower required for the purpose will be huge and managerial dimensions
of handling such work force will require further manager level workforce.
Committee’s further observation
3.2 The Committee is of the firm view that a permanent office at district level for electoral
roll revision is necessary as this activity is of continuous nature. The Government needs to review
their stand in the light of Committee’ s recommendations. These offices can be set up on trial basis,
as suggested by the Committee. The Committee therefore impresses upon the Government to take
necessary action in this regard.

18
Recommendation/observation
ELECTORS PHOTO IDENTITY CARDS (EPIC)
4. The Committee is perturbed to know that 28% are yet to be issued/covered under
the EPIC programme. The Committee feels that the Election Commission has not achieved
the desired goals despite the fact that considerable time has elapsed since the inception of
the EPIC scheme. The Committee understands that for being photographed at a particular
Centre, only few selected dates are announced and are hardly publicised. If a voter for
whatever reasons, fails to get him photographed during that period, he is not issued EPIC.
If a provision is made for being photographed on all working days during the revision of
rolls, the problem can be solved to a great extent. The Committee, therefore reiterates its
earlier recommendation that the Commission should devise a time-bound programme for
achieving 100% EPIC coverage and make a provision for getting photographed of the voters
on all working days while revising the rolls. (Para 5.24)
Action Taken Reply
4.1 The Election Commission has taken note of the concern expressed by the Committee to
maximize the EPIC coverage. To maximize the EPIC coverage, normally special field campaigns at
Designated Photography Locations (DPL) are carried out with publicity. The periods of campaigns,
which are generally dependent on number of residual electors in the area has been increased. The
scale of publicity to such campaigns is also increased further. In fact, the Commission has also
allowed alternate method of submission of photographs already available with the residual electors
for getting EPIC. Thus, it is continuous method and there are no off-days for preparation of EPIC.
4.2 To address the situation, the Commission has also directed the States to establish permanent
EPIC Centres to function round the year. However, the Commission reiterates that unless EPIC is
made compulsory document, the EPIC coverage will have some shortfall.
Committee’s further observation
4.3 The Committee’ s concern shall remain unanswered as the Ministry did not categorically state
as to by when 100% coverage under EPIC programme will be achieved. The Committee would
certainly like to know what targets have been set out by the EC in this regard and how the
problems in this regard would be overcome.
4.4 The Committee however appreciates the measures being taken by the EC for maximizing the
EPIC coverage. But going by this pace, much has to be achieved. The Committee therefore
impresses upon the Election Commission for a time bound programme to be undertaken.
Recommendation/observation
THE INSTITUTE OF LEGISLATIVE DRAFTING AND RESEARCH
5. The Committee is happy to note that ILDR had organized a training programme on
Legislative Drafting in which participants from 13 countries of the world participated.
Similar courses may also be run for the participants coming from the different States
including the officers of both the Houses of Parliament and State Legislatures and
reiterates its earlier recommendation that the Institute should devise a proper fee structure
for running these courses. Also that the Institute should not confine itself to imparting
training in the Country only, rather it should think on expanding its area outside India. The
Committee also recommends that the Institute should try to explore means by which
legislative drafting can be made popular and done in other regional languages so that it can
greatly benefited by the State Governments. (Para 5.36)

19
Action Taken Reply
5.1 In this connection, it may be mentioned that since the year 1988, when the cabinet decided
to establish the Institute of Legislative Drafting and Research (ILDR) for the purpose of providing
training for the officers of States and Union territories there is no fees for the trainee officers
coming from States/Union territories. There is no fee for the trainee officers of foreign countries.
Earlier foreign trainees came for two weeks but last year, it reduced to only one week. In fact,
foreign trainees come to the Institute due to and under an arrangement made by the Bureau of
Parliament Affairs. The Institute may take steps for expanding its area when the same starts
functioning in full fledged manner in its own building.
5.2 With regard to legislative drafting in Regional languages, it may be mentioned that,
preparation for providing training for legislative drafting in Hindi in the Institute is under active
consideration by this Department.
Committee’s further observation
5.3 The Committee feels that the Institute would run in full swing only when it gets its own
campus which is yet to be set up. The Committee also feels that institute should make all out
efforts imparting training in other regional languages in addition to Hindi.
Recommendation/observation
CENTRALLY SPONSORED SCHEME RELATING TO INFRASTRUCTURAL FACILITIES FOR
THE JUDICIARY
6. The Committee feels that the Centrally Sponsored Scheme relating to infrastructural
facilities though started with zeal has suffered due to lack of planning. Moreover, State
Governments have failed miserably to provide their share. The Committee therefore
recommends that there should be proper monitoring of the scheme in terms of achievement
of the targets, allocation of funds etc. This is because even the basic infrastructural facilities
like transport and housing are not available to the Judicial Officers at lower judiciary level
and they have to face many difficulties. These infrastructural related issues hamper the
functioning of the Judicial Officers. The Committee, therefore, reiterates its earlier
recommendation that the Ministry should consider all these components seriously and include
them in the perspective plan. The Committee opines that the focus should be on achieving
targets earmarked and relax the means of achieving them in so much as even funding 100%
for the schemes in question and sees no difficulty in development of infrastructure for
transport facilities and then handing it over to the administration branch of State Government
for further regulation so that they can function more effectively. (Para 6.24)
Action Taken Reply
6.1 The development of infrastructure facilities for the judiciary is being implemented as a
Centrally Sponsored Scheme on a 50:50 basis between the Central and State Governments since
the inception of the scheme in 1993-94. Under the scheme, the central share is determined by the
Planning Commission and budget provision for that financial year is provided to the State
Government who are under an obligation to put in from their own resources at least an equal
amount as their share. The Union Territories are not required to match the Central share provided.
The scheme is being continued in the Eleventh Five Year Plan on the same basis as approved by
the Planning Commission, earlier.
6.2 At the stage of finalization of the Eleventh Plan outlay for the scheme, a proposal was made
to the Planning Commission for incorporating a component of transport facilities for the judicial

20
officers as part of the scheme as recommended by the Committee. The Planning Commission has,
however, not included this as part of the scheme.
6.3 The total outlay for the scheme for the Eleventh Five Year Plan is Rs.701.08 crore. This
scheme is exclusively for construction of court buildings and residential accommodation for the
judges and judicial officers. In the period from 1993-94 to 2007-08, an amount of Rs.894.30 crore
had been released to the States and UTs as central share.
6.4 In the year 2007-08 as against a Budget Estimate of Rs.65 crore, Government provided a
total amount of Rs.103.80 crore by making re-appropriation of funds, thus ensuring that the States
have more funds for implementing the scheme.
6.5 The budget provision for 2008-09 is Rs.133 crore which is considerably higher than the
budget provision for the year 2007-08.
6.6 Government attaches utmost importance to the implementation of the scheme and monitors
the utilization of the funds allocated and released to the States/UTs as also the physical progress
through the UCs and progress reports furnished by the States.
Committee’s further observation
6.7 The Committee appreciates the enhanced budget allocation for the current year. The
Committee is however constrained to note that the Department of Justice have not informed the
Committee of measures taken to motivate the State Governments who have failed to contribute their
share under this scheme. The Committee would like to have the information in respect of all the
States covered by this scheme along with the details of monitoring mechanism ensuring the effective
implementation of the scheme; the targets set, their achievements and the expenditure made in the
last three years and the relaxation, if any, given to the States in this regard.
Recommendation/observation
FAMILY COURTS
7. The Committee express its disappointment with the pace of establishment of Family
Courts in the country. It feels that the Ministry should take up the matter with State
Governments and fix a target for establishing at least one Family Court in each district so
as to resolve family disputes and related matters expeditiously and if need be amend the
relevant provision of the Family Court Act, 1984 pertaining to eligibility criteria of
population exceeding one million for setting up of a family court, so that at least one family
court is set up in each district particularly. (Para 6.33)
Action Taken Reply
7.1 In so far as the matter of establishing more Family Courts is concerned, Minister for Law
and Justice has written to the Chief Ministers/Administrators of all State Governments/Union
Territories pursuant to a request received from the Chief Justice of India that Family Courts may
be established in all Districts of the country.
7.2 The Government has also written to the State Governments requesting for the cost
estimates for setting up such Family Courts.
7.3 A number of States and UTs have responded over a period of time. While some Chief
Ministers have informed that they are having the matter looked into, the Governor of Karnataka
informed that the matter was under consideration of the High Court. The Chief Minister of West
Bengal has informed that steps are being taken to establish Family Courts in five Districts in

21
consultation with the High Court of Calcutta, his Government having decided to set up Family
Courts in the remaining Districts. The Chief Minister of Delhi has mentioned that the matter of
setting up of Family Courts is under active consideration of a Committee of Judges in the Delhi
High Court, the premises for setting up of Family Courts at two locations is likely to be ready
shortly. The Chief Minister of Maharashtra has informed that his State agrees in principle to set
up Family Courts in all the Districts and the concerned High Court has identified eleven places
where Family Courts can be set up. The Government of Rajasthan has informed that fourteen
Family Courts are to be set up.
7.4 The Administrator of UT of Andaman and Nicobar Islands has informed that the
infrastructure for a court building for the Family Court has already been built and a proposal is
shortly being submitted for establishing Family Court. The Administrator of the UT of Chandigarh
has informed that they are awaiting the framing of the rules by the State of Punjab that is expected
to be completed shortly.
7.5 The Chief Minister of Arunachal Pradesh has mentioned that the State does not have a
single town or city whose population exceeds one million and also that all family disputes are
settled as per customary and personal law of the indigenous population of Arunachal Pradesh.
Establishment of Family Courts in Arunachal Pradesh is not considered necessary.
7.6 The Government of Goa has mentioned that it has no town or city having a population of
one million. All matters pertaining to family disputes are being dealt with by regular civil courts
(senior divisions) in accordance with the common civil code applicable throughout the State
irrespective of caste, race, religion and that there appeared to be no requirement for establishment
of Family courts in the State of Goa.
Committee’s further observation
7.7 The Committee feels that with this speed, it will take long time to set up at least one family
court in each district. Responses from the State/UT Governments are not very encouraging as only
a very few of them have initiated the process. The Committee impress upon the Department of
Justice to vigorously pursue this issue with all the State and UT Governments to set up family court
in each district. The Committee desires that Government may explore the possibility as to how the
process can be expedited.
Recommendation/observation
PENDENCY OF CASES
8. The Committee notes with concern that year after year, the pendency of cases has
been steadily increasing. The trend is continuing even after taking recourse to other
alternative measures like setting up of fast track courts, family courts and permanent Lok
Adalats. The Committee has also been apprised that the Government has been constantly
reviewing accumulation of the arrears in Courts and the problem is sought to be tackled
by constitution of specialized benches and organizing Lok Adalats at regular intervals;
encouraging alternative modes of disposal, establishing Fast Track Courts even at the level
of Magistrates Court etc. The Committee finds that specialized. (Para 6.42)
8.1 Lok Adalats and Fast Track Courts, though created as an alternative mode of
disposal of arrears of cases, have been suffering due to infrastructural lacunae or financial
constraints and thus are not able to meet the desired targets. The Committee hopes that
with the establishment of Gram Nyayalayas the pendency will come down drastically. The
Committee therefore reiterates its earlier recommendation that the Ministry should
carefully analyze the factors responsible and look for viable solutions in addition to the

22
existing arrangements. The Committee further desires that since the pendency is mounting
by the day despite various measures taken in that regard, the Government, should request
the Law Commission of India to look into the whole gamut of the problem in an holistic
manner with help of ILI and Research Departments of Law Universities and submit its
Report as expeditiously as possible. (Para 6.43)
Action Taken Reply
8.2 The Committee’s recommendation that the Ministry should carefully analyze the factors
responsible for increasing pendency is one which has been the concern of the Government for
quite some time. Various Committees in the past have gone into the question of arrears, delay in
disposal and pendency of cases in courts. The Law Commission has also gone into the question
of pendency of cases in courts and made recommendations in this regard in the 77th and 79th
Report given in 1979 and 124th Report given in 1988. The Terms of Reference of the 18th Law
Commission inter-alia include “to keep under review the system of judicial administration to ensure
that it is responsive to the reasonable demands of the times and in particular to secure elimination
of delays, speedy clearance of arrears and reduction in costs so as to secure quick and economical
disposal of cases without affecting the cardinal principle that decisions should be just and fair”.
In view of this, the matter of requesting the Law Commission to look into the whole gamut of
the problem of pendency in a holistic manner is being examined in the Department.
8.3 Further, the Department has taken up a new Plan scheme which is shortly to be taken up
for approval in the Standing Finance Committee. This scheme proposes a component of studies by
reputed institutions in the country like the Indian Law Institute, research departments of various
Law Universities on different facets of judicial reforms including one on causes of increasing
pendency and measures to be taken to reduce it. This initiative of the Government is likely to fulfil
the Committee’s desire mentioned in Para 6.42.
Committee’s further observation
8.4 The Committee takes note of the initiative taken by the Government to address the problem
of pendency of cases. However, the reply does contain the details of new plan scheme. The
Committee directs the Department of Justice to furnish the details of scheme.
Recommendation/observation
V ACANCY OF JUDGES
9. The Committee notes with concern that there has not been any worthwhile
improvement with regard to filling up of vacancies of Judges in Supreme Court and High
Courts. The Committee impresses upon the Ministry to immediately take steps to fill the
remaining vacancies so that the same can help in reducing the mounting level of cases at
various levels. The Committee, therefore, calls upon the Ministry to come forward with an
alternative like the pre 1993 arrangement by involving the Executive, instead of allowing
the judiciary alone to choose the Judges. The aspirants of various vacancies should be
allowed to apply and appear before the Selection Committee. The closed system prevailing
now is not getting meritorious persons called to the Bench. Transparency, inclusiveness and
merit should be the way of appointing Judges. Till the warrant of appointment is issued by
President of India, it is maintained as secret. It is against democratic principles. The
aspirants’ names, merit and selection process should be made public and transparent,
through the High Court and Supreme Court website. The Report, at various levels in
Departments of Justice and Home and other stages, should be on the website of their
department till the final stage of issuing warrant of appointment. (Para 6.46)

23
Action Taken Reply
9.1 Filling up of vacancies in the High Courts is a continuous process. Vacancies do keep
arising on account of retirement, elevation or resignation of Judges. The Central Government has
been making every effort to fill up the existing vacancies in the Supreme Court and High Court.
The Minister of Law and Justice has been periodically reminding the Chief Justices of the High
Courts, to initiate proposals for filling up all vacant posts of Judges in the High Court. The
proposals received by the Department are processed expeditiously for approval of the competent
authority.
9.2 The existing system of appointment of Judges of Supreme Court and High Courts is in
pursuance of Supreme Court Judgment dated October 6, 1993 in the Supreme Court Advocates-
on Record and Anr vs. Union of India read with the Advisory Opinion of October 28, 1998. Any
change in the present system would require amendment of the Constitution or a review of their
judgment by a larger Bench of Supreme Court. There is at present no proposal before the
Government for bringing any change in the system of appointment of Judges.
9.3 It is the view of the Department as taken in the court that the records of deliberations
between the Chief Justice of India, Minister of Law and Justice, Prime Minister are in the nature
of advice tendered by the Cabinet to the Hon’ble President and hence, being privileged, cannot be
disclosed.
9.4 So far as making the appointment process transparent is concerned, it is the view of the
Department that public disclosure of names of candidates during the appointment process may be
an impediment in the dispassionate consideration of the names.
Committee’s further observation
9.5 The Committee is not convinced with the reply given by the Department of Justice. The
Committee has already addressed the issue of appointment, accountability and transparency in
appointment of Judges of Supreme Court and the High Courts in its 21st Report on ‘Judges
(Inquiry) Bill, 2007’, 27th Report on ‘Action Taken Replies on Law’ s Delays: Arrears in Courts’,
and 28th Report on ‘Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Amendment Bill: 2008’ and impressed
upon the Government to take necessary steps in restoring the pre-1993 arrangement by involving
the executive.
9.6 In its report on ‘Judges (Inquiry) Bill, 2007’ the Committee suggested for bringing a
comprehensive legislation not only providing for the appointments of Judges by entrusting the
appointment to a body other than the collegium with representation both from the judiciary and the
executive. The Committee is of the considered opinion that it could be entrusted to the proposed
“Empowered Committee” which could initially screen the names and thereafter, refer the same to
the National Judicial Council for final recommendations.
9.7 Similarly the Committee in its 27th Report recommended for the restoration of the primacy
of the Executive in the matter so that judicial vacancies are filled up promptly and expeditiously.
9.8 Again in its 29th Report the Committee stressed on the Government to ensure the
compliance to the recommendations of the Committee in its previous Reports. The Department of
Justice while furnishing their action taken reply to the Committee’ s recommendation (para 6. 5)
stated:
“The appointment of Judges of the High Court and Supreme Court is being made in
accordance with the Supreme Court’ s judgment of October 26, 1993  and their Advisory
Opinion of October 28, 1998.  Any Change in the present system may required amendment
of the Constitution. The matter is being examined in the Department.”

24
9.9 The Committee takes note of the reply furnished by the Ministry. It is noteworthy that the
Law Commission of India, in its 214th Report, widely endorsed the recommendations of this
Committee in this regard. The Committee gathers that following the recommendations of the
Committee, the Government is pondering to review the existing system of appointment of Judges
in Supreme Court and High Courts as the collegium system has failed. The Committee strongly feels
this is the time the Government should take initiative. The Committee therefore hopes that
Government will now give due consideration to the Committee’s recommendations made in its
reports to save the judiciary by strengthening transparency and accountability regime to which it
has prime status and respect of the citizens.
Recommendation/observation
INCOME TAX APPELLATE TRIBUNAL [ITAT]

Recommendation/observation
NATIONAL LEGAL SERVICES AUTHORITY [NALSA]
11. The Committee notes that its recommendation in [20th Report on the Demand for
Grants [2008-09], that more and more States and UTs should raise the income-ceiling limit for

the enhancement was not upto the level of competitiveness. The Committee therefore,
recommends that the fee structure of Legal Aid Counsels should be suitably enhanced so

rationalization of fee structures along with the follow up action taken by the State authorities. The

26
Committee desires that NALSA may analyse whether it has resulted in competent lawyers assisting
the beneficiaries on the basis of input data made available by the State authorities. The Committee
directs the Ministry to furnish these details to the Committee.

empowerment of all the sections of the society, yet certain grey areas need to be addressed

implementation of the schemes and programmes of NALSA. The Committee, therefore,
recommends that the Ministry should send fact-finding teams in the States to have on the

13.2 The Committee finds that reply given by the Ministry is not satisfactory as it does not
clearly state to what extent the problem of non-utilisation or under utilisation of grants has been
addressed, what has been the outcome of the initiatives taken by the State authorities. The

notes.
Recommendation/observation
14. The Committee has been apprised by the Ministry that there is no scope for evolving
any Centrally Sponsored Scheme with component to provide hundred percent funding by the
Centre for operationalising NALSA’s plans since under the provisions of the Legal Services

Recommendation/observation
DELINKING OF DEPARTMENT OF JUSTICE FROM THE MINISTRY OF HOME AND
CREATION OF A SEPARATE DEPARTMENT OF JUSTICE WITH A FULL TIME SECRETARY
OF JUSTICE
3. The Committee feels that the rationale behind keeping Department of Justice under
the control of Home Secretary was logical at the time when this decision was taken during
the year 1971 but in view and of the drastic changes in last ten fifteen years, the rise in
the incidents of terrorism, birth and growth of naxalism in the country; the growing
complexity of modern crimes, handling natural calamities throughout India are becoming
difficult for the Home Secretary to devote time specifically for the Department other than
the Home. In nearly all the Government Departments there is a separate post of Secretary
to carry out the work of the Department in an efficient manner. Moreover, the Department
of Justice has been assigned a distinct task under the Government of India (Allocation of
Business) Rules, 1961, and the Department has been performing sensitive functions
pertaining to judicial appointments, service conditions of Judges and the administration of
justice. Viewed in this context and also of the fact that there are about 3 crore cases
pending in different Courts and about 100 High Court vacancies are to be filled and
thousands of vacancies exist in subordinate judiciary, thus corroding the faith of the people
in the judicial system, it would be more appropriate if the Department is accorded a distinct
identity including strong administrative structure of its own. It is in this context that the
Committee is of the considered opinion that for the sake of administrative efficiency and
exigency, the Department is separated from the Home Ministry and provided with a full-
fledged Secretary. (Para 6.12)
Action Taken Reply
3.1 The administrative efficiency and the service delivery of the Department of Justice have not
been compromised on account of the Department not having an independent Secretary and the
Home Secretary also being the Secretary of the Department. As has been mentioned earlier in
respect of the 20th Report, though the administrative arrangements of the Department of Justice
are through the Ministry of Home Affairs, the Department of Justice is an independent Department
delinked and separated from the Home Ministry in terms of its functions and functional
independence as also in respect of budgetary allocations for both Plan and Non Plan schemes. The
Department of Justice is implementing Plan and Non Plan schemes for improvements in
administration of justice independent of any restrictive/budgetary control from the Home Ministry.
These schemes are aimed at reducing the pendency of cases in the courts and facilitating
improvements of efficiency of courts. Reduction of pendency is a matter predominantly within the
domain of the judiciary. Filling up vacancies in the subordinate judiciary is a matter with which
State Governments are concerned. These are matters which are not affected by the Department not
having an exclusive separate Secretary. On the contrary since the Ministry of Home Affairs is
responsible for Criminal Laws such as Indian Penal Code and Criminal Procedure Code and for
Prisons, it is advantageous to the Department of Justice to have the Home Secretary also as the
Secretary of Justice, more so as a lot of coordination is often required between the judiciary, the
police as also the prisons. Further the Ministry of Home Affairs is responsible for issuing advisories

31
to the State Governments and thus having the Home Secretary as Secretary (Justice) facilitates
better coordination with State Governments. The fact of the Home Secretary also heading the
Department of Justice as Secretary allows the Department of Justice leverage while dealing with
the other Ministries and Departments of the Government. This considerably facilitates the resolution
of issues and problems for the Department of Justice. The Department of Justice often needs and
use the services of agencies which work under the Ministry of Home Affairs. The fact of Home
Secretary as Secretary (Justice) facilitates cooperation of these agencies in the performance of
tasks assigned to the Department of Justice.
3.2 In view of the above distinct advantages in having the Home Secretary also as Secretary
of the Department of Justice, the Committee is requested not to press for a change in the existing
arrangement.
Committee’s further observation
3.3 The Committee is not in agreement with the view of the Government and still firmly
believes that Department of Justice has to be independent of the control of Ministry of Home
Affairs and needs to be headed by separate Secretary. The Committee is however constrained to
observe that Government has not given any weightage to the Committee’ s recommendations made
in this regard.
3.4 The Committee strongly believes that judicial administration is all together different affair
than the general administration and it needs to be managed by a professional who is exclusively
trained and experienced in handling judicial matters. Contrarily, the Justice Department has been
deprived of independence in managing its own affairs. Instead, the government of India has
preferred to club this department with the Home Ministry depriving to have a separate Secretary,
as nearly all the Government Departments have, to carry out the work of the Department in an
efficient manner and thereby ignoring the distinct task it has to perform under the Government of
India (Allocation of Business) Rules, 1961, and the sensitive functions pertaining to judicial
appointments, service conditions of Judges and the administration of justice.
3.5 The Committee further observes that the Central Government provides for the grants for
development and regulation of judiciary and the funds from International Institutions are also
earmarked for certain institutions/activities. Besides, there is a strong need for making more funds
available to judiciary by enabling the Supreme Courts and the High Courts to generate revenue
themselves which can also be utilized by the subordinate judiciary in the States. Further, the
vacancies in the Supreme Court and the High Courts remain un filled for a long time which needs
to be filled in on the date of retirement as it can be closely monitored and planned in advances.
Judicial reforms have to be implemented. The Committee feels that such matters calls for instant
and continuous involvement of the Head of the Department. The Home Secretary being the incharge
of Internal Security supervises the law and order in the country. Besides this he is involved in
numerous responsibilities like managing natural calamities and because of this he does not find
enough time to manage the affairs of Justice Department. It is in this context the Committee
recommends that Justice Department must be headed not only by separate Secretary but also
professional, exclusively trained in judicial matters.
Recommendation/observation
BENCHES OF THE SUPREME COURT
4. The High Court benches in various places in addition to the State capital is much
appreciated by people for easy accessibility to justice to the poor and needy, on reasonable
expenditure. The Committee is not happy with the persistent opposition for establishing

32
benches of the Supreme Court in other parts of the country without advancing any
convincing reason or justification therefore. Even the Constitution of India makes
provisions for it under Article 130 of the Constitution. The Committee, therefore, endorses
its earlier view that establishment of benches of the Supreme Court atleast in Chennai on
trial basis and then in other parts of the country would be of immense help to the poor who
cannot afford to travel from their native placed to Delhi. The Committee, therefore, feels
that the Ministry should come forward with a necessary Constitutional amendment to
address this deadlock. (Para 6.51)
Action Taken Reply
4.1 Article 130 of the Constitution provides that “the Supreme Court shall sit in Delhi or in such
other place or places as the Chief Justice of India may, with the approval of the President, from
time to time, appoint”.
4.2 The matter of setting up of Supreme Court Benches outside Delhi has been taken up the
Chief Justices of India from time to time, However, the Supreme Court has not agreed to setting
up of Bench of Supreme Court at any place outside Delhi. The Chief Justice of India, in his letter
dated 12th August, 2007, informed that after reconsideration of the matter, the Full Court, in its
meeting held on 7th  August 2007, found no justification for deviating from its earlier resolutions
on the subject.
4.3 The Supreme Court of India have recently introduced a system enabling the Advocates-on-
Record/petitioner-in-person to file cases in the Supreme Court of India through internet to obviate
the difficulties faced by the litigants.
4.4 The recommendation of the Committee is being examined in consultation with the Ministry
of Law and Justice.
Committee’s further observation
4.5 The Committee reiterates its recommendations vide para 6.51  of 26th Report. However, the
report and action taken as per para 4 of the action taken reply is awaited. The Committee will
like to make its observation in the light of that report.

and’” the Universities without taking these short comings into proper consideration grant affiliation
to such institutions.
13.2 When the matters come before the Bar Council of India it becomes difficult for the Council
to deal with these colleges as they resort to litigation. In spite of this unpleasant situation, Bar
Council of India has been taking utmost care in granting approval of affiliation to new law colleges.
BCI’s policy is to weed out sub-standard law colleges and establish only institutions which have
adequate infrastructure for imparting proper legal education. They have been advocating for
reintroduction of training for law graduates before their enrolment. In fact they had introduced
such a scheme some time ago but the scheme was challenged in various High Courts in the
country and ultimately the Hon’ble Supreme Court struck down the scheme on the ground that the
Advocates Act does not empower the Bar Council of India to prescribe a training programme for
law graduates as a pre condition for enrolment. Bar Council of India suggests that necessary
amendments in the advocates Act be carried out to enable the re- introduction of pre enrolment
training to the law graduates.
Committee’s further observation
13.3 The Committee expresses its concern over the deteriorating standard of legal education
throughout the country and is not satisfied by the efforts being made for improving the standard.
The Committee strongly feels that Bar Council of India has a definite role to play in checking the
mushrooming growth of Law Colleges without adequate infrastructure. The BCI must not allow such
colleges to have affiliation with it. BCI should also approach the State Governments impressing
upon them to check the growth of such colleges.
13.4 As regards the issue of training for the lawyers before entering the profession, the Committee
impresses upon the Ministry to bring out a bill proposing requisite amendment in Advocates Act.
Recommendation/observation
INSTITUTE OF CONSTITUTIONAL AND PARLIAMENTARY STUDIES (ICPS)
14. As it appears, there is total lack of co-ordination between the Ministry and the ICPS,
which is disappointed. The Committee, therefore, exhorts the Ministry that it should take
all out efforts to bridge cordial co-ordination with agencies under its administrative control.
The Committee recommends that the Ministry should take up the issue with the concerned
agencies and the Secretariats of Parliament who are facing space crunch and may share the
costs in case some space is provided to them and ensure that the construction work is
started at the earliest. The Committee also direct Ministry to furnish a status report at the
time of Action Taken Reply. The Committee further recommends that Institute of
Constitutional and Parliamentary Studies (ICPS) should regularly organize capsule courses
in Parliamentary Privileges, Debates, Questions etc. for the benefit of newly elected
Member of Parliament. (Para 4.61)

14.1 ICPS Building — As this Department has already informed to Hon’ble Committee that a

The meeting ended with the understanding that a detailed proposal for Grant-in-aid in this regard

will be submitted by the ICPS which will be considered in this Department as per the rules relating
to Grant-in-aid. The ICPS has recently submitted a draft EFC proposal for sanction of funds for
construction of building for ICPS in some detail to this Department on June 17, 2008. The same
is being examined in this Department.
14.2 Capsule Courses– As recommended by the Committee, ICPS has planned to organize
following capsule courses for the benefit of elected MPs. It is proposed to invite senior — i.e.,

14.3 The secretarial assistance in preparation of materials is being explored before the dates can
be finalized. If ICPS get relevant authorizations and funds from within or outside the Institute, they
may be able to hold the programmes as follows:
Topic T entative Dates
1. Parliamentary Privileges During Monsoon Session — August – September, 2008
2. Questions and Debates During Winter Session — December, 2008
3. Election Laws Budget Session — February, 2009
Committee’s further observation
14.4 The Committee takes note of the status report on the action taken in respect of construction
of building for ICPS. However, the Committee is worried over the inordinate time being taken by
the Ministry in the matter. The Committee would like to review the progress in the matter at the time
of consideration of demands for grants of the Ministry. The Committee hopes that by then the

Department and Director, ICPS and impressed upon them to take initiative in the matter. In the

14.8 The Committee expects that the Ministry of Urban Development will facilitate the ICPS and
